messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hairdresser
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 54

She is a 19-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who works as a hairdresser, and when she first begins speaking about what happened, she does so carefully, as if approaching something sharp. She has been in a relationship for about a year, and her boyfriend is one of the few people she still lets see how badly this has shaken her. Before the incident, she describes herself as lively, talkative, and proud of the way she could make people feel better about themselves at the salon. She liked the rhythm of the work, the smell of shampoo, the small intimacy of standing behind someone’s chair and helping them leave feeling more confident.

The event that changed her happened on an ordinary workday, which is part of what makes it so hard for her to hold in mind. It was not dramatic at first. She was on her way out after work, tired and thinking about an argument she had been having with her boyfriend earlier that week. There was a moment of distraction, a sudden movement, and then a collision she still replays in fragments. A person was seriously injured because of her mistake. She says the worst part is not only that it happened, but that it happened in an instant, before she had time to understand what she had done. She remembers the sound, the panic, and the expression on the other person’s face. Even now, the image returns without warning, and she feels her body tighten as if she is about to be pulled back into that moment.

In the days afterward, she cannot stop running the scene through her mind. She wakes with it, thinks about it while washing her hands, and finds herself staring into space at work as the memory takes over. At first she tells herself she needs to be strong and keep functioning, but the effort of holding herself together leaves her exhausted. She starts sleeping poorly, jolting awake from vivid dreams in which the injury happens again but this time she cannot stop it. She begins to dread nighttime because the house gets quiet and her thoughts get louder. She lies awake listening for sounds outside, increasingly aware of her heartbeat and breathing, as though her body has not gotten the message that the danger is over.

Returning to the salon is harder than she expects. The first few times she stands at her station, her hands feel clumsy and unreliable. She worries about making a mistake with scissors, about dropping a tool, about being the reason something goes wrong again. She becomes unusually tense around noise in the shop, jumping when someone calls her name from behind or when a hairdryer suddenly turns on. The bright mirrors and close contact with clients, which once felt comforting, now sometimes make her feel trapped. She notices herself scanning the room, calculating exits, and feeling embarrassed when a small sound makes her flinch. On the outside she continues to smile and answer politely, but inside she is braced for something bad to happen.

She also begins to change in the way she thinks about herself. Before, she saw herself as competent and caring. Now she feels contaminated by what happened, as if one terrible action has erased every good thing she has done. She says she keeps wondering what kind of person can hurt someone by accident and still deserve to have a normal life. This guilt is not abstract; it follows her into ordinary moments. When her boyfriend tries to comfort her, she often pulls away because she cannot bear feeling cared for while believing she has done something unforgivable. At times she becomes irritable with him and then feels ashamed for that too. Other times she goes quiet for hours, sitting with her arms wrapped around herself, trying not to cry because once she starts she fears she will not stop.

Her relationships at home have narrowed. She avoids talking about the incident with family because she does not want to see their concern or risk their judgment. She keeps herself busy with work, scrolling on her phone during breaks or cleaning equipment she has already cleaned, anything to stay occupied and not think. Still, the memories break through. She is startled by sudden braking on the road, by raised voices, by anything that resembles the sounds around the accident. When that happens, she feels as if she is back there again, not remembering but reliving. Afterward she is drained and shaky, often needing to sit alone in the staff room until she can steady herself.

Over time, she has become quieter, less spontaneous, and more guarded with her trust. She still goes to work, still does clients’ hair with skill, but she no longer feels like the same girl who once moved through her days so easily. She describes moving through life with one part of her always looking backward, waiting for the moment when the memory catches up to her again.
